transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-01-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kumar (Redwood SE); Michael Torres (Head of ML, TideWave), Sara Li (Infra Lead), Ravi Patel (PM)

Summary:
Quick scoping call for a 4-week POC to validate TideWave Payments' primary LLM workload: real-time payments routing assistant and reconciliation heuristics. Focus on workload characterization (QPS, concurrency), token distributions, success criteria (latency & accuracy), and a benchmark plan. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, VPC requirements, and next steps for data sharing and baseline benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- POC success criteria (latency P95, cost per 1M tokens, qualitative accuracy)
- Workload sizing: steady vs peak QPS, concurrency expectations
- Input/output token distribution and prompt composition (chat vs single prompt)
- Benchmark plan and synthetic load parameters
- Deployment model options: hosted vs dedicated/VPC
- Security/compliance: SOC2, KMS, retention windows

Action items (short): see metadata for owners/due dates.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect - "KV cache" sometimes appears as "K-V cash", "SAML" as "sam-el"):

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to run through TideWave's workload and agree on success criteria for the POC. Priya will own the bench side, I'll handle pricing/security follow ups. Michael, do you want to kick off with a bit of context on the feature set?

[00:20] Michael Torres: Yeah sure, um so our main two use cases are a payments routing assistant that helps ops route ambiguous transactions and a reconciliation assistant that suggests likely counterparties. Most of the traffic is triggered by user queries in our ops console; so it's fairly chatty, um maybe a lot of short back-and-forths.

[00:40] Ravi Patel: To add, typical session starts with a 1-2 sentence system prompt (meta context), then 2-5 user messages. We also have some batched reconciliation jobs that hit the embedding/summary endpoints.

[01:05] Priya Kumar: Helpful. Do you have approximate QPS/peak numbers? Even ballparks are great.

[01:14] Michael Torres: On average right now about 30 QPS, but we see spikes to 200 QPS during morning settlement windows, those last for maybe 10-15 minutes. Concurrency at peak looks like roughly 120-150 concurrent sessions.

[01:35] Alex Chen: Okay that's useful. For planning the POC we usually model both steady-state and 99th percentile spikes. So if peak is 200 QPS, we'd test at 200 and maybe a 2x stress at 400 to understand headroom.

[01:54] Sara Li: Quick question on tokens — what's the token distribution per request? We have some prompts that are long, like a full transaction history snippet.

[02:05] Michael Torres: Most single interactions are small: avg input tokens ~120, avg output ~240. But the reconciliation batch jobs can have inputs of 800-2k tokens (we'd chunk those), and outputs vary. Overall rough distribution: 85% are chat-style requests under 500 tokens total, 15% are long batch or document summarizations.

[02:37] Priya Kumar: Great. For Redwood's benchmarking and modeling we'll ask for a histogram or some sample logs, but those numbers are already enough to size an initial bench.

[02:50] Alex Chen: Success criteria — what would make the POC a win for TideWave? Michael?

[02:58] Michael Torres: Primary is latency — for the ops console we target p95 < 300ms ideally, but we'll accept up to 400ms if cost is reasonable. Second is correctness/accuracy — recon suggestions must meet our current heuristic baseline, we'll provide a small eval set. Third is clear cost math: we need to understand $/1M tokens and projected monthly spend at scale.

[03:28] Priya Kumar: Good, we'll include latency targets and cost estimates in the plan. One tip: latency numbers depend a lot on model choice, quantization profile, and whether you run hosted or dedicated infrastructure.

[03:45] Ravi Patel: On deployment — we have strict data residency and want VPC peering or private deployment. We also need KMS integration for keys. Is that supported for POC?

[03:58] Alex Chen: Yes, for POCs we can do a VPC peering flow with Redwood Hosted control plane or spin up a private deploy depending on the scope. We'll need Sara to confirm IAM and network contacts. We also have SOC2 docs and an infra checklist we'll send.

[04:15] Sara Li: Perfect — we will want to see audit logs and retention settings too.

[04:25] Priya Kumar: Now on traffic modeling: we'll produce a synthetic load plan that mirrors your distribution. For your steady 30 QPS and peak 200 QPS we typically run 3 phases: baseline steady (30 QPS 30 min), peak replay (200 QPS 15 min), and stress (400 QPS 5-10 min) to validate graceful degradation and fallbacks.

[04:50] Michael Torres: Does Redwood do prefix caching or KV cache for multi-turn chats? That's important because a lot of our sessions reuse context.

[04:58] Priya Kumar: Yes, Redwood supports KV cache and prefix caching; in practice we see effective per-token cost reductions if prompts are highly repetitive. We'll instrument to measure cache hit rate during the bench.

[05:15] Alex Chen: Also will explore batching. Some of the reconciliation jobs are highly batchable — we can run those on a different route with larger batch sizes to optimize cost.

[05:28] Ravi Patel: For benchmarking models, which models do you recommend for our use case? We can't use OpenAI in production due to data policy, so prefer open models or private variants.

[05:40] Priya Kumar: We'll start with two model families: a smaller low-latency 7B-quantized variant for the ops console and a larger 13- or 34-B model for higher-quality reconciliation tasks. We'll also run a fallback variant for cost/lower-latency tradeoffs. We'll document models, quantization, and expected cost/latency profiles.

[06:05] Michael Torres: How will you measure accuracy? We'll provide an eval set — do you support automatic evals?

[06:12] Priya Kumar: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes basic eval harnesses; for the POC we'll run the eval set through each candidate model and give precision/recall-like metrics for reconciliation and a small human-reviewed sample for conversation quality.

[06:30] Alex Chen: Bench specifics — Priya, can you outline the benchmark steps so Michael/Sara know what artifacts you'll need?

[06:40] Priya Kumar: Sure. Step 1: get sample traffic + prompt templates. Step 2: define scenarios (steady, peak, batch jobs). Step 3: run synthetic load with real prompt payloads at target QPS and record latency P50/P95/P99, errors, and token counts. Step 4: run accuracy eval on withheld set. Step 5: produce report with recommended model/quantization/config and cost estimate. We generally run a 1-hour sweep for each scenario to get stable metrics.

[07:10] Sara Li: For the VPC peering flow, timeline? We have change windows but can work with Redwood.

[07:18] Alex Chen: Usually peering + infra review takes 3-5 business days. For the POC we can do peering; if timeframe is tight we can also run a secure hosted lane with stricter retention and KMS. We'll include both options in the plan.

[07:33] Ravi Patel: What about monitoring and dashboards during POC? We need token-level costs and latency breakdowns per route.

[07:40] Priya Kumar: Redwood Console will expose per-route latency, token counts, and cost estimates. We'll share temporary access for the pilot.

[07:50] Michael Torres: Any gotchas on multi-tenant vs dedicated? Our compliance folks prefer dedicated for isolation.

[07:58] Alex Chen: Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput and isolation, but has a higher commit. For a 4-week POC we usually test on hosted or a temporary dedicated pool. We'll put numbers in the cost sketch so you can evaluate.

[08:12] Priya Kumar: One more technical note: long context requests (800-2k tokens) will benefit from different kernel paths and sometimes need different batching; we'll note that in the bench. Also quan-tiza-tion profiles can change latency characteristics, so we test at the quantized and full precision runs.

[08:32] Michael Torres: Sounds good. On success criteria again — p95 latency <300ms, quality within our eval threshold, and cost within projected budget. If those hit we move into a 60-day pilot and then rollout.

[08:47] Alex Chen: Great, we'll treat those as formal success criteria. We'll also include a fallback plan if latency doesn't meet target (model change, dedicated pool, or cache tuning).

[09:00] Ravi Patel: Can you also include a simple cost sensitivity table — like cost at 30 QPS steady, cost at 200 QPS peak, and projected monthly spend at 200k monthly active sessions?

[09:12] Alex Chen: Yes — that'll be part of the pricing sketch.

[09:20] Michael Torres: Any required credentials or access we need to give you for the bench? We can give S3 links with sample prompts or a short SQL extract.

[09:28] Priya Kumar: S3 link or redacted logs is perfect. Also a small eval CSV with ground truth for reconciliation.

[09:35] Sara Li: We'll prepare those and aim to share by Tue (2026-01-13).

[09:40] Alex Chen: Cool. Timeline recap: data share by 2026-01-13, benchmark run and initial results by 2026-01-18, pricing/security docs by 2026-01-14, pilot kickoff week of 2026-01-26, 4-week POC through late February. Does that align with everyone?

[09:58] Michael Torres: Yes that works for us.

[10:05] Priya Kumar: I'll prepare the bench plan and share the template after the call. We'll include scripts, workloads, and expected metrics.

[10:15] Alex Chen: OK, we'll also send SOC2 and the infra checklist. Any final questions?

[10:22] Ravi Patel: None from me.

[10:24] Sara Li: All good.

[10:26] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[10:30] End meeting.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-attributions and ASR errors expected; treat numeric values as approximate until bench results confirm.
